_meta.basis: Adult dosing. AHA 2025 Guidelines for CPR & ECC (ACLS), NASEMSO National Model EMS Clinical Guidelines, TCCC. Fictional county protocol.
_meta.status: DRAFT — requires review by a paramedic/EMS educator before release. Effect magnitudes marked TUNE are gameplay-tuned, not clinical values.
rules: Every drug is physically in the box at every cert level. Nothing is hidden or locked.
Vials show only what a real vial shows: name, concentration, volume. No indications in-game.
scopeLevel = the minimum cert level legally allowed to give it. Giving it below scope is ALLOWED but logged as a scope-of-practice violation in the debrief.
Dose math: player draws up mL. mL = dose_mg / concentration_mg_per_mL. Wrong concentration = wrong dose, with real consequences.
Effects apply over onset -> peak -> duration curves, never instantly (except adenosine, which is near-instant and brief).
pk_s: route -> [onset_s, peak_s, duration_s]. Engine curve anchors (approximate adult values). 0 duration = continuous while running.
controlled: DEA schedule. Controlled drugs live in narcotics_safe: sign-out, count and waste are logged; discrepancies are flagged in the debrief.
location: which bag/box the item is physically stored in (jump_bag, airway_bag, drug_box, narcotics_safe, rsi_kit, iv_cabinet, cc_box, blood_cooler, cbrn_kit, ob_kit, onboard).
Pediatric dosing beyond the few noted entries is NOT yet included; slice patients are adults.
coverage: antibiotic activity 0-3 per organism class. Engine multiplies infection growth by (1 - coverage match vs the infection's organismProfile). Time-to-first-antibiotic is logged.
_meta.effectScale: Effect tokens: '+', '++', '+++' / '-', '--', '---' = relative magnitude. Engine maps tokens to numbers in physiology.json (TUNE).

drugs.name: Epinephrine

presentations.label: Epinephrine 1 mg/10 mL (0.1 mg/mL) prefilled syringe

dosing.max: no ceiling in AHA (local protocols may cap)
dosing.notes: Shockable: give after first failed defibrillation. Nonshockable: give as early as possible. IV preferred over IO. Use the 0.1 mg/mL concentration.
1 mg/mL concentration, anterolateral thigh. 0.3 mg via auto-injector.
Requires dilution to 10 mcg/mL. Paramedic/CC skill.
Titrate to effect when atropine fails.
1 mg/mL x 5 mL nebulized (alternative to racemic). Observe for rebound.

dangers: CLASSIC ERROR: pushing 1 mg/mL IV in a patient WITH a pulse = severe hypertension, VT/VF, MI, stroke. Model this.

drugs.name: Amiodarone

dosing.notes: IV push in arrest. Alternative to lidocaine (AHA 2025 treats them as reasonable alternatives).
Then infusion 1 mg/min. Requires a pulse — DO NOT push rapidly in a patient with a pulse.

contraindications: Marked sinus bradycardia or high-degree AV block without pacemaker
dangers: Hypotension with rapid infusion in a perfusing patient

drugs.name: Lidocaine

presentations.label: Lidocaine 100 mg/5 mL (20 mg/mL) prefilled syringe

dosing.notes: Alternative to amiodarone.

route: IO slow over 2 min before flush
dosing.notes: 0.5 mg/kg max 40 mg. Conscious patients find IO infusion extremely painful — the AI patient should scream without it.

dangers: Toxicity >3 mg/kg: altered mental status, seizures, bradycardia, arrest

drugs.name: Adenosine

route: IV rapid push + 20 mL NS flush
dosing.repeat: 12 mg if no conversion in 1-2 min
dosing.notes: Most proximal large-bore IV (AC). Run a rhythm strip. Patient will feel 'impending doom' — the AI patient should react.
Only if regular AND monomorphic.

effects.rhythm: brief asystole/pause then conversion if reentrant SVT

contraindications: Irregular wide-complex tachycardia (AFib with WPW) — can trigger VF
2nd/3rd degree AV block or sick sinus without pacemaker
dangers: Slow push or distal IV = drug degrades before heart, no effect
Reduce dose: heart transplant, dipyridamole, carbamazepine, central line

drugs.name: Atropine

presentations.label: Atropine 1 mg/10 mL (0.1 mg/mL) prefilled syringe

dosing.notes: If ineffective: pacing, or epinephrine/dopamine infusion. Will NOT work on denervated (transplanted) heart. Less effective in Mobitz II / 3rd-degree with wide QRS.

dosing.repeat: double q5 min until secretions dry
dosing.notes: Large doses expected. Endpoint = drying of bronchial secretions, not HR.
Peds only, selective use.

contraindications: NOT for PEA/asystole (removed from arrest algorithm)
dangers: Doses <0.5 mg may cause paradoxical bradycardia
Tachycardia increases O2 demand in ACS

drugs.name: Norepinephrine

dosing.notes: Titrate to MAP ≥65 (post-ROSC target SBP ≥90 / MAP ≥65).

dangers: Masks hemorrhagic shock if used instead of volume/blood

drugs.name: Vasopressin

dosing.notes: Critical care only.

dangers: NOT part of the 2025 AHA cardiac arrest algorithm — epinephrine is the only vasopressor. Giving it in arrest is logged as non-guideline.
drugs.gameRole: Realistic distractor for the arrest scenario.

dosing.notes: Typical adult ~15-20 mg, then ~20-25 mg.

drugs.name: Verapamil
contraindications: Same as diltiazem; never in wide-complex tachycardia or WPW
dangers: More negative inotropy than diltiazem; reversal: calcium
drugs.gameRole: Present as an alternative; most EMS boxes carry diltiazem instead.

dosing.notes: Stop when: arrhythmia suppressed, hypotension, QRS widens >50%, or max dose reached. Maintenance 1-4 mg/min.

drugs.name: Magnesium Sulfate

presentations.label: Magnesium sulfate 50% 1 g/2 mL (500 mg/mL) vial

dosing.notes: Some protocols 4-6 g load.

dangers: Rapid push in perfusing patient = hypotension, flushing
Toxicity: loss of reflexes → respiratory depression; reversal: calcium

drugs.name: Sodium Bicarbonate

presentations.label: Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 50 mEq/50 mL prefilled syringe

dosing.notes: Then infusion; target urine alkalinization. CC.

contraindications: Routine use in cardiac arrest — NOT recommended
dangers: Precipitates with calcium in same line (flush between)
drugs.gameRole: Routine use in arrest without hyperkalemia/TCA cause is logged as non-guideline.

drugs.name: Calcium Chloride 10%

presentations.label: Calcium chloride 10% 1 g/10 mL (100 mg/mL) prefilled syringe

dosing.notes: FY26 JTS: after the first unit of blood, then every 4 units. Or calcium gluconate 3 g.

dangers: Severe tissue necrosis if extravasated — large proximal vein

drugs.name: Calcium Gluconate 10%

presentations.label: Calcium gluconate 10% 1 g/10 mL (100 mg/mL) vial

dosing.notes: ~1/3 the elemental calcium of chloride; safer peripherally.

dangers: Under-dosing if treated as equivalent to chloride

dosing.notes: 4 x 81 mg. Range 162-325 mg.

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin

dosing.notes: Get IV access first if possible (Paramedic). 12-lead before first dose (check right-sided V4R in inferior STEMI).

contraindications: PDE5 inhibitor: sildenafil/vardenafil within 24 h, tadalafil within 48 h
RIGHT VENTRICULAR INFARCT (inferior STEMI with ST elevation V4R)
dangers: RV infarct + nitro = preload-dependent heart loses preload → profound hypotension/crash. Model this — it's the signature trap.

dosing.notes: Weight/protocol max ~0.1 mg/kg.

drugs.name: Fentanyl

presentations.label: Fentanyl OTFC lozenge 800 mcg (TCCC)
presentations.notes: OTFC was removed from TCCC guidelines; some kits still carry it. Do not re-dose without direction.

dosing.notes: Typical adult 25-100 mcg. IN via atomizer. Preferred over morphine in hypotension-risk patients.

dangers: Rapid high-dose IV: chest wall rigidity

drugs.name: Ketamine

dosing.notes: TCCC favors for casualties in shock — no BP drop.
Some protocols 2-4 mg/kg IM. Requires monitoring and airway readiness.

dangers: Emergence reactions (AI patient dialogue goes weird — good feature)

drugs.name: Midazolam

dosing.notes: Adults >40 kg. 5 mg if 13-40 kg. IV 0.1 mg/kg alt. Repeat once if still seizing after 5-10 min.

dangers: Respiratory depression, especially combined with opioids/alcohol

drugs.name: Rocuronium
contraindications: No airway plan / cannot intubate-cannot oxygenate risk
dangers: PARALYTIC WITHOUT SEDATION = awake paralysis (major error)
Paralyzing without being able to ventilate = death. Model this.
Long duration — no spontaneous recovery in a failed airway

drugs.name: Succinylcholine
contraindications: Hyperkalemia or suspected (renal failure, crush injury)

drugs.name: Naloxone

presentations.label: Naloxone 2 mg/2 mL (1 mg/mL) prefilled syringe

dosing.notes: TITRATE TO RESPIRATORY DRIVE (RR ≥10, adequate ventilation), NOT full wake-up. Ventilate with BVM first.

duration.all: ~30-90 min — SHORTER than many opioids. Re-sedation is real.

dangers: Over-dosing → acute withdrawal: vomiting, agitation, combativeness, refusal of transport (AI patient should do this)

dosing.repeat: recheck glucose in 5-10 min; repeat 10 g aliquots

drugs.name: Dextrose 50% (D50)

presentations.label: D50W 25 g/50 mL (0.5 g/mL) prefilled syringe

dangers: Severe tissue necrosis on extravasation — why many systems switched to D10

drugs.name: Oral Glucose Gel
contraindications: Cannot protect airway / cannot swallow / unresponsive
dangers: Aspiration if given to a patient who can't protect airway

dosing.notes: Paramedic/CC. Often causes vomiting.

drugs.name: Diphenhydramine

dosing.notes: Adjunct only — does NOT replace epinephrine in anaphylaxis.

dangers: Using this INSTEAD of epi in anaphylaxis is a critical error

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
dangers: No acute effect — player shouldn't expect improvement on scene

drugs.name: Tranexamic Acid (TXA)

route: IV/IO in 100 mL NS over 10 min
dosing.notes: TCCC: 2 g slow IV/IO push acceptable. Must be within 3 h of injury. FY26 JTS ERC: 2 g IV/IO if not already given and within 3 h.

dosing.repeat: 1 g after 30 min if bleeding continues

dangers: Giving >3 h post-injury logged as error

drugs.name: Ketorolac
dangers: Giving to a bleeding trauma patient worsens hemorrhage — trap

drugs.name: 0.9% Sodium Chloride (Normal Saline)

dosing.notes: Reassess lung sounds after each bolus.
PERMISSIVE HYPOTENSION: titrate to palpable radial pulse / SBP ~80-90. EXCEPTION — TBI: avoid any SBP <90, target ≥110.

dangers: Over-resuscitation in trauma 'pops the clot' → re-bleeding
Feeds the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy)

dosing.notes: Same permissive hypotension rules. Less acidosis than NS. Do not run with blood in same line.

drugs.name: Low-Titer O Whole Blood (LTOWB)

dosing.notes: TCCC preferred resuscitation fluid. Give calcium with/after first unit. Use a fluid warmer.

dangers: Cold blood worsens hypothermia without warmer

drugs.name: Oxygen

dosing.notes: Titrate SpO2 94-98% (88-92% in known COPD retainers).
1 breath q6 s (10/min) with pulse; 30:2 or 1 q6 s with advanced airway during CPR.

dangers: Hyperoxia in ACS/stroke/post-ROSC with SpO2 already normal (logged as overtreatment)
Running out of O2 — tank pressure is tracked

presentations.label: Phenylephrine 10 mg/1 mL vial (dilute to 100 mcg/mL for push dose)

dosing.notes: Requires 1:100 dilution. Common post-induction hypotension rescue.

drugs.name: Nitroglycerin IV

dosing.notes: Start 10-20, titrate q3-5 min.
High-dose nitro with CPAP. CC.

contraindications: Same as SL nitroglycerin: hypotension, PDE5 inhibitors, RV infarct

drugs.name: Labetalol

dosing.notes: Stroke lytic candidate target <185/110. Aortic dissection: HR <60 and SBP <120.

dangers: Overcorrection of BP in stroke = extended infarct

dosing.notes: Then 50-300 mcg/kg/min infusion.

drugs.name: Heparin (unfractionated)

dosing.notes: Then 12 units/kg/h, max 1000 units/h.

dangers: Giving to a trauma patient = catastrophic

dosing.notes: Hospital/MSU only. Requires CT.
Only where the receiving cath lab protocol requests it. Plus aspirin.

drugs.name: Furosemide

dosing.notes: Most modern protocols removed it: nitro + CPAP are first line.

dangers: Many 'CHF' patients are actually pneumonia/sepsis or not volume overloaded
drugs.gameRole: Realistic legacy drug. Using it before nitro/CPAP is logged as non-preferred.

drugs.name: Digoxin Immune Fab
dangers: Calcium in dig toxicity was historically feared ('stone heart') — model as controversial

dosing.notes: ~5-7x morphine potency. 0.015 mg/kg.

drugs.name: Nitrous Oxide 50:50

dosing.notes: Patient must hold the mask themselves (safety: drops it when sedated).

dangers: Giving to the bike-down patient with a developing pneumo makes it tension faster — trap

drugs.name: Lorazepam
dangers: Slow IM absorption — midazolam preferred IM

drugs.name: Diazepam
dangers: IM absorption erratic — don't give IM

drugs.name: Propofol

dosing.notes: Rarely prehospital — hypotension.

dangers: Profound hypotension in shocked patients — trap vs ketamine/etomidate

drugs.name: Dexmedetomidine
dangers: Bradycardia, hypotension; slow onset — not for emergencies

drugs.name: Sugammadex
contraindications: Does NOT reverse succinylcholine or benzos/opioids
dangers: Reversing paralysis doesn't save you if sedation is still on board and the airway is lost
drugs.gameRole: Rescue option for a failed RSI with rocuronium.

drugs.name: Droperidol
dangers: QT prolongation (boxed warning; clinically rare at EMS doses)

drugs.name: Haloperidol

dosing.notes: 2-5 mg in elderly. Often combined with midazolam (B52 = haldol + benadryl).

dangers: Slow onset vs ketamine for excited delirium

drugs.name: Olanzapine ODT
dangers: IM olanzapine + parenteral benzo = respiratory depression

drugs.name: Racemic Epinephrine 2.25%
dangers: Rebound stridor 2-4 h later — must transport

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone

dosing.notes: Peds 2 mg/kg max 100. Patient/family often carries their own emergency kit — the AI family member should mention it if asked.

dangers: Missing adrenal crisis → refractory hypotension unresponsive to fluids/pressors — trap

drugs.name: Activated Charcoal
dangers: Aspiration pneumonitis if patient vomits with AMS

drugs.name: Hydroxocobalamin

presentations.label: Cyanokit 5 g vial (reconstitute with 200 mL NS)

dangers: Turns skin, urine and plasma red — interferes with colorimetric labs
drugs.gameRole: House-fire victim with normal SpO2 but crashing = cyanide (SpO2 reads normal). Also CO: SpO2 falsely normal.

drugs.name: Atropine/Pralidoxime Auto-Injector

presentations.label: DuoDote: atropine 2.1 mg + pralidoxime 600 mg auto-injector

dosing.notes: SLUDGEM/DUMBELS + miosis. Plus atropine IV titrated until secretions dry. Plus benzo for seizures.

dangers: Scene safety: decon FIRST or the crew becomes patients

drugs.name: Pralidoxime

dosing.notes: Always with atropine. Time-sensitive (aging).

dangers: Rapid push → laryngospasm, muscle rigidity, tachycardia

drugs.name: Flumazenil
dangers: Precipitates refractory seizures in benzo-dependent or TCA co-ingestion — classic trap
drugs.gameRole: Most EMS systems don't carry it. Giving it in an unknown overdose is logged as a critical error.

dosing.notes: Then 0.25 mL/kg/min. Repeat bolus x2 for persistent instability. LAST: lidocaine/bupivacaine toxicity.

drugs.name: Methylene Blue 1%

presentations.label: Methylene blue 50 mg/10 mL (5 mg/mL) vial

dangers: Pulse ox reads ~85% regardless of O2 in metHb — model the lying pulse ox

drugs.name: Thiamine

dosing.notes: Don't delay dextrose in hypoglycemia to give thiamine first.

dangers: Delaying dextrose to give thiamine = critical error

dosing.notes: Plus vitamin K (hospital). Some flight programs carry.

drugs.name: Promethazine
dangers: Boxed warning: IV extravasation/intra-arterial → gangrene, amputation — trap

drugs.name: Famotidine
dangers: Adjunct only — never instead of epinephrine

drugs.name: Tetracaine 0.5% Ophthalmic
dangers: Pressure on an open globe extrudes contents

drugs.name: Acetaminophen PO (TCCC Combat Wound Pill Pack)

dosing.notes: 2 tabs q8h. TCCC pairs with meloxicam 15 mg.
Minimal platelet effect at this dose — why TCCC allows it in combat wounds.

drugs.name: Cefazolin

dosing.notes: 3 g if >120 kg. Earlier = fewer infections.

drugs.notes: No anaerobe coverage: wrong drug alone for fecal contamination.

drugs.name: Ertapenem (TCCC)
drugs.notes: FY26 JTS: post-surgical if not already given. Covers fecal flora (gram-negative + anaerobes).

drugs.name: Moxifloxacin (TCCC)
drugs.notes: Former TCCC combat-wound PO antibiotic. Superseded in TCCC by cefadroxil/cephalexin PO (FY26 JTS ERC). Still on some kits.

drugs.name: Ceftriaxone

dosing.notes: FY26 JTS ERC first line when unable to take PO. Also penetrating eye trauma.

dangers: Precipitates with calcium-containing fluids (LR) in same line

dosing.notes: Signs: blown pupil, posturing, GCS drop ≥2, Cushing's triad.

drugs.name: Mannitol 20%
dangers: Hypotension in the bleeding trauma patient — hypertonic saline preferred — trap

drugs.name: Oxytocin

dosing.notes: Or 10-40 units in 1 L NS titrated. Plus fundal massage.

dangers: Given before second twin delivered = trapped fetus / uterine rupture — trap

dosing.notes: Prehospital plasma improved 30-day survival in air-medical transport (PAMPer). Calcium with blood products.
Pair with plasma (1:1). PRBCs alone don't fix coagulopathy.

drugs.name: Dextrose 5% in Water (D5W)

dosing.notes: Diluent for some infusions (amiodarone drips). NOT a resuscitation fluid.

dangers: Bolusing D5W in shock or TBI is logged as a critical error
drugs.gameRole: Realistic distractor in the IV cabinet.

drugs.name: Piperacillin-Tazobactam
dangers: Penicillin-allergic patient: anaphylaxis risk (check the history card)

drugs.name: Vancomycin

route: IV over 1-2 h (≥1 g/h max rate)

dangers: Infused too fast → vancomycin infusion reaction (flushing, hypotension)
No gram-negative coverage: pair with another agent

drugs.name: Clindamycin
dangers: Stops toxin production in nec fasc / toxic shock, but must be paired with broad coverage

dosing.notes: FY26 JTS ERC recommended PO agent.
Covers Pasteurella, Eikenella, anaerobes. Usually ED-started; CC/PFC only.
FY26 JTS: give if available and not previously given.
FY26 JTS: then 1000 mg q12h. Status epilepticus second-line 60 mg/kg max 4.5 g (hospital/CC).
